sounds.intro: Uyghur is written right to left in an Arabic-based alphabet that marks every vowel. The Latin shown is the Uyghur Latin spelling. There are no genders and no articles. The stress is usually on the last syllable.
rows: say "oh" with rounded lips, like German "ö"
say "ee" with rounded lips, like German "ü"
a "k" made far back in the throat
notes: Vowel harmony: back vowels (a, i, o, u) and front vowels (e, é, ö, ü) are not mixed in one word. Suffixes follow the same rule.
The Arabic-script line is written by rule from the Latin. Where a word starts with a vowel, the script shows the letter hamza first.

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Uyghur often drops the pronoun, because the verb ending shows who is speaking. There is no he / she difference: "u" means both.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: Add -lar or -ler, by vowel harmony. After a number, the noun stays singular: ikki kitab (two book).

grammar.title: To be: -men, -sen, -miz
text: There is no separate verb "to be". Add an ending to the noun or adjective. Uyghur also uses "-dur" for "he / she is".

grammar.title: Bar and yoq: have, there is
text: Uyghur says "my X exists" (bar) or "my X does not exist" (yoq). The ending shows the owner: -im (my), -ing (your), -i (his).

grammar.title: Present tense: -watimen
text: Verb stem + -wati + person ending. Kélish (to come): kél-iwati-men.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb goes last. Order: who, where or when, what, verb. Uyghur has no articles: "kitab" means "a book" or "the book".

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put -ma / -me after the verb stem: barimen (I go), barmaymen (I do not go). For nouns use "emes" (is not). "Yoq" means "there is not". Always compare with the positive form.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Add the little word -mu after the word you are asking about. It is the same for every question.

grammar.title: Question words
text: Question words stand where the answer would stand.

grammar.title: Possessives and liking
text: Endings go on the noun: -im (my), -ing (your), -i (his / her). To say you like something, use "manga yaqidu" (to me it is pleasing).

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: sen (informal): friends, family, children. siz (formal): strangers, older people, work. Verb endings change: -sen (informal), -siz (formal).

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: -di + person ending (bardim = I went). Future uses the present form with a time word: ete barimen (tomorrow I go).

grammar.title: Commands
text: Informal: the bare verb stem. Formal: add -ing (kéling). To forbid, add -ma / -me after the stem.

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: Can: verb + -alaymen (yüzelaymen, I can swim). Must: "kérek" (needed). Want: -moqchimen (barmoqchimen, I want to go).
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Uyghur uses endings, not words in front: -da / -de (in, on, at), -gha / -ge / -qa / -ke (to), -din (from), -ning (of).
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Put "téximu" before the adjective for "more": téximu chong. For "the most" put "eng" before it: eng chong. "Than" is -din.
